assessments.reasoning: The displayed cover names W. Kirk Snyder, New York University's Courant Institute, September 9, 1990 and Technical Report 490. The Computer History Museum site preserves the author's report, whose abstract identifies its reference and operation-manual parts. Directly reacquired exact PDF SHA-256 94abc989ed6667c2684648ec15048bcf368ae8d9bbffd8948167424afc288372. Its rendered print pages, pypdf extracted text, decoded page streams and exact cited passage offsets reproduce. The rendered headings and exact passage at §1.3.1 Write Parameter Restriction, printed p. 3 (physical PDF p. 9) address the frozen proposition. §1.3.1 explicitly ties first-class status to all-read-only formal parameters and denies an assignable procedure value if any formal is read-write or write-only. The adjacent discussion distinguishes storing a procedure from calling it and storing its return value. The authority is the report’s 1990 documentation of SETL2 and its then-current implementations. The edition and facet stay bounded to the registered revision. The mixed-mode example is legal when called directly and does not establish an assignable value. The procedure-value entry confirms the restriction and separately limits serialization and arithmetic, without affecting the asserted first-class status.

challenge.method: Read the write-parameter example and the value-versus-call contrast across printed pages 2–3. Cross-check the declared parameter modes, mixed-mode direct call and the formal procedure-value entry on printed pages 14 and 16.
challenge.results: The mixed-mode example is legal when called directly and does not establish an assignable value. The procedure-value entry confirms the restriction and separately limits serialization and arithmetic, without affecting the asserted first-class status.

limitations: The restriction concerns using a procedure itself as a value. Ordinary direct calls and procedure return values have separate rules.
The report describes the restriction for this language design. It does not make an unrestricted claim about every operation on a first-class value.
